newsitem.title: INDIA: Hostages' families appeal to Kashmir worshippers.
newsitem.headline: Hostages' families appeal to Kashmir worshippers.

text.p: Relatives of three of four Westerners taken hostage in Kashmir more than a year ago appealed to Moslem worshippers at the region's holiest shrine on Friday for clues to the captive tourists' fate.
"Let us know where our men are, please," they said in a pamphlet distributed to worshippers at Hazratbal shrine on the outskirts of Srinagar, summer capital of India's Jammu and Kashmir state.
American Donald Hutchings, German Dirk Hasert and Britons Paul Wells and Keith Mangan were captured by little known Al-Faran guerrillas while trekking in the Himalayan region in July last year.
Indian officials and diplomats say they do not know whether the four men are dead or alive.
Norwegian Hans Christian Ostroe, who was also kidnapped in July last year, was later found beheaded.
Mangan's mother Mavis and wife Julie, Wells' girlfriend Catherine Mosley and Hutchings' wife Jane Schelly handed out the pamphlets, written in Urdu, to women worshippers at the shrine.
Barefooted, wearing local dress and their heads covered with scarves in deference to Moslem tradition, the Western women tied threads and photographs of the hostages to the main gate of the shrine.
Kashmiri Moslems customarily tie threads to the gates of shrines in hope of receiving blessings and seeing their needs fulfilled.
"Please help them. They are in search of their sons and husbands," Bashir-u-Din, chief priest of the Hazratbal shrine, told worshippers over loud speakers.
Meanwhile, hardcore militants who Indian authorities claim are linked to the kidnapping appealed on Friday for the release of the tourists.
The Harkat-ul-Ansar group delivered a statement in Urdu to local newspapers in Srinagar, summer capital of India's Jammu and Kashmir state.

"If any militant group has abducted them as the Indian media is projecting, we appeal to them that if they are true Moslems, for God's sake and for the betterment of Kashmir's freedom movement, they should release them immediately," it said.
"We are extremely thankful to hostage families who visited Sikender's house and expressed sympathy with the bereaved family," the Harkat-ul-Ansar statement said.

On Fridays, thousands of Moslems offer prayers at the shrine, which believers say houses a hair from the beard of the Prophet Mohammad. Jammu and Kashmir is mainly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state.
"It is disgusting, shameful for the whole community if we have held their men in captivity," Raja Begum, a woman worshipper, told Reuters. "We shall make every effort to get them released."
Bob Wells and Charles Mangan, fathers of the British hostages, distributed pamphlets among the men.

"Please help us, we are feeling lonely without them," Bob Wells announced from the loud speakers of the shrine. "If they are alive, release them. And if they are dead, please return their bodies so that we can observe their last rites."
Frustrated by the absence of any firm information about the hostages, their relatives have scoured the Kashmir valley this week for clues.
On Wednesday, they met the mother of a dead militant, Sikender, who authorities said was part of the Harkat-ul-Ansar group, accused by the Indian government of being linked to the kidnappings.
